title: Final Accounts: Meaning, Objectives and the Trading Account
summary: What final accounts are, why they are prepared, and how to prepare a trading account to find gross profit with a worked example.

p: Final accounts are the financial statements prepared at the end of an accounting period (usually a year) to show the profit or loss and the financial position of a business. They come from the trial balance and adjusted ledger balances.

Objectives: to find the net result (profit or loss); to show the financial position; to help owners, lenders and managers to decide; to meet legal and tax rules; to give information to investors and lenders.
Three statements for a sole trader or partnership: the Trading Account (gross profit), the Profit and Loss Account (net profit) and the Balance Sheet (position).
It shows the gross profit or gross loss from buying and selling goods. Gross profit = Net sales – Cost of goods sold (COGS).
Net sales = Sales – Returns inwards (goods customers sent back).
Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases (less returns outwards) + Carriage inwards – Closing stock. (Carriage inwards, the cost of bringing goods in, is part of the cost of the goods.)

sections.h: Worked example (the question in the notes)
p: Sales ₦200,000; opening stock ₦30,000; purchases ₦100,000; carriage inwards ₦10,000; closing stock ₦20,000.

head: Trading account for the year ended 31 December

p: The lesson note's trading account mixes the 'Net Sales' and 'Cost of Goods Sold' lines in the wrong columns. The vertical layout above is clearer and is accepted by examiners. In the T-account layout, opening stock, purchases and carriage inwards are on the debit side; sales less returns inwards on the credit side; the closing stock is shown as a deduction (or on the credit side); the balancing figure is the gross profit carried down.
Gross profit as a percentage of sales = 80,000 ÷ 200,000 × 100 = 40%. It helps to compare years.

title: Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet
summary: Finding net profit, the layout of a vertical balance sheet, and a corrected solution to the balance sheet assignment.

p: It starts with the gross profit and adds other incomes (discount received, commission received, rent received) and takes away all running expenses (salaries, rent, electricity, stationery, depreciation). The result is the net profit or net loss. Net profit = gross profit + other income – expenses.
A balance sheet shows the assets, liabilities and capital at a date. Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

Fixed assets (non-current): land, buildings, furniture, machines. Current assets: stock, debtors, bank, cash. Current liabilities: creditors, bank overdraft. Capital: opening capital + net profit – drawings = closing capital.

Trial balance items: opening stock 30,000; purchases 100,000; carriage inwards 10,000; salaries 15,000; rent 8,000; stationery 2,000; furniture 30,000; debtors 60,000; cash 50,000; drawings 10,000; sales 200,000; creditors 20,000; capital 95,000 (the balancing figure). Closing stock ₦20,000.
Trading account: gross profit ₦80,000 (as before). Profit and loss: expenses 15,000 + 8,000 + 2,000 = 25,000; net profit = 80,000 – 25,000 = ₦55,000.

sections.h: The balance sheet assignment: a data error
p: The assignment gives capital ₦150,000, drawings ₦10,000, net profit ₦40,000, creditors ₦20,000, cash ₦50,000, debtors ₦60,000, stock ₦70,000 and furniture ₦30,000. Assets = 30,000 + 70,000 + 60,000 + 50,000 = ₦210,000. Capital side: 150,000 + 40,000 – 10,000 = 180,000, plus creditors 20,000 = ₦200,000. The two sides differ by ₦10,000, so the balance sheet cannot balance as the question is written.

This is an error in the lesson note, not your mistake. A simple repair that gives a balanced sheet: creditors ₦30,000. Then the capital side is 180,000 + 30,000 = ₦210,000 and it balances. In an examination, always check that assets equal capital plus liabilities, and tell the examiner if the figures do not agree.

Accrued expenses (owed but not paid) and prepaid expenses (paid in advance). Depreciation of fixed assets. Provision for bad debts. Closing stock. These affect both the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet. Example: rent paid ₦8,000 includes ₦1,000 prepaid. Rent expense in the P&L = 7,000; prepaid rent 1,000 is a current asset.

title: Regulation of the Capital Market: Bodies and Their Functions
summary: What capital market regulation is for, and the roles of the SEC, NGX, CBN, PenCom and CAC.

p: Capital market regulation is the laws, rules, bodies and procedures that supervise and control the market. Its aims: protect investors; keep the market fair and open; keep the financial system stable; prevent fraud, insider trading (using secret information to trade) and price manipulation.
Ensure market integrity. Protect investors. Promote confidence. Help the market to grow. Enforce standards of disclosure and honest conduct.

The apex regulator of the capital market, set up under the Investments and Securities Act. Functions: registers and licenses capital market operators; approves public offers, mergers and takeovers; watches trading to stop manipulation; enforces the rules and punishes offenders; educates investors.

Formerly the Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE). It is a self-regulatory organisation: it runs the market where securities are traded. Functions: provides the trading platform and listing services; makes sure companies meet listing rules; suspends or removes companies that break the rules; monitors trading and reports unusual activity.
Mainly the monetary authority, but it indirectly affects the capital market by supervising banks that take part in it and by keeping the financial system stable.
It regulates how pension funds are invested in the capital market, so that retirement savings are safe.
It registers companies and enforces the Companies and Allied Matters Act, ensuring proper incorporation and corporate governance.

title: Laws, Importance and Challenges of Capital Market Regulation
summary: The laws and rules that regulate the market, why regulation matters, and its challenges and solutions.

p: The Investments and Securities Act (ISA); the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA); the NGX listing rules; SEC rules, guidelines and circulars; the Nigerian Code of Corporate Governance; and the anti-money laundering laws. Note: the ISA has been updated by a newer Act; check the current name and year on the SEC website.

It prevents fraud and insider trading. It builds investor confidence, so more people take part. It makes the market more stable. It protects minority shareholders (those with few shares) from being cheated by big owners. It enforces disclosure and openness. It encourages ethical business.
Weak enforcement of the laws. Insider trading and other dishonest practices. Poor investor knowledge. Slow court cases. Weak technology for watching the market.
Keep reforming the laws; educate investors; use digital systems to watch the market; punish offenders quickly and fairly; train regulators.

A director learns that his company is about to be taken over at a high price and buys shares secretly before the news is public. This is insider trading. The SEC can fine him, order him to give up the profit and take him to court. The rule protects other investors, who did not have the information.
1. Prevents fraud. 2. Protects investors. 3. Builds confidence. 4. Promotes stability. 5. Ensures openness and honest reporting.

title: Hire Purchase and Instalment Payment: Meaning and Differences
summary: What hire purchase and instalment payment (credit sale) are, who owns the goods, and how they differ.

p: Many individuals and businesses acquire goods without paying the full price at once. Two common methods are hire purchase and instalment payment. Both let the buyer use the goods at once and pay over time, but ownership and the accounting treatment differ.

The buyer takes the goods at once but becomes the legal owner only after the last instalment is paid. Features: payments are made by instalments; interest is usually charged; the seller keeps ownership until full payment; if the buyer defaults the seller can take the goods back (repossess); the buyer can usually return the goods before full payment; hire purchase is regulated by law (the Hire Purchase Act and similar laws).

The buyer becomes the owner as soon as the contract is made but pays by instalments. If the buyer fails to pay, the seller cannot take the goods back but may sue for the money. The buyer bears all the risk from delivery, may not return the goods unless defective, and may pay interest.
Study the table.

head: Feature
Hire purchase
Instalment payment
rows: At once, when the agreement is made
No, must complete the payments or be sued
Buyer bears all risk after delivery

p: Cash price: the price if paid in full at once. Deposit: the first payment made by the buyer. Hire purchase price: the total paid by the buyer = deposit + instalments (this is higher than the cash price). Instalments: regular payments. Interest: the extra cost for paying over time = hire purchase price – cash price. Balance due: what is left after the deposit.

Hire purchase: advantages: immediate use; payment spread; helpful when capital is small. Disadvantages: higher total cost; risk of repossession; ownership delayed. Instalment payment: advantages: immediate ownership; fixed repayments; suits creditworthy buyers. Disadvantages: the buyer bears all risk from day one; legal action on default; goods cannot be returned.

sections.h: Why a seller may prefer hire purchase
p: The seller keeps ownership, so the goods can be taken back if the buyer does not pay. That is why sellers like hire purchase for expensive goods such as vehicles and machines, while a credit sale depends on trusting the buyer.

title: Accounting for Hire Purchase (Buyer's Books)
summary: A corrected worked example with the journal entries, the hire vendor account and treatment of interest, and the solutions to the questions.

p: The lesson note's example says cash price ₦200,000, deposit ₦50,000 and 3 yearly payments of ₦50,000 'which include interest'. But 50,000 + 3 × 50,000 = ₦200,000, the same as the cash price, so there is no interest at all. A real hire purchase costs more than the cash price. We therefore use a corrected example.

Cash price of equipment ₦200,000. Deposit ₦50,000. Three yearly instalments of ₦60,000. Hire purchase price = 50,000 + 3 × 60,000 = ₦230,000. Interest = 230,000 – 200,000 = ₦30,000 (₦10,000 a year, shared equally for simplicity).
Study the table.

Balance after purchase: 200,000. After the deposit: 150,000. Year 1: + 10,000 interest = 160,000; – 60,000 = 100,000. Year 2: + 10,000 = 110,000; – 60,000 = 50,000. Year 3: + 10,000 = 60,000; – 60,000 = nil. The account is cleared at the end, and total interest of ₦30,000 has been charged to the Profit and Loss Account over three years. In real life, interest is charged on the unpaid balance each year, so it falls as the balance falls.

The buyer treats the equipment as his own asset from the start, and depreciates it on the cash price, for example 20% a year: ₦40,000 a year. Dr Depreciation expense 40,000; Cr Provision for depreciation 40,000.

Question 5: hire purchase of ₦120,000 with deposit ₦40,000 and two annual instalments of ₦40,000. The total paid is 40,000 + 80,000 = ₦120,000, the same as the price, so there is no interest. Entries: Dr Equipment 120,000, Cr Hire vendor 120,000; Dr Hire vendor 40,000, Cr Bank 40,000; year 1 and year 2: Dr Hire vendor 40,000, Cr Bank 40,000.

Assignment 3: furniture worth ₦180,000 bought with ₦60,000 down and three yearly instalments, total payments ₦210,000. Interest = 210,000 – 180,000 = ₦30,000. Each instalment = (210,000 – 60,000) ÷ 3 = ₦50,000.
Treatment of interest: the interest is not part of the cost of the asset. It is an expense of each year in which it arises and is charged to the Profit and Loss Account.

title: Accounting for Instalment Purchases and a Comparison Table
summary: The journal entries when ownership passes at once, and a table comparing hire purchase and instalment payment under five headings.

p: Ownership passes at once, so the asset is recorded at the cash price, and the seller is a creditor. At purchase: Dr Asset account (cash price); Cr Creditor (cash price). Each payment: Dr Creditor; Cr Bank. Interest for the period: Dr Interest expense; Cr Creditor (or Bank, if paid with the instalment). The lesson note says to debit the asset with the 'total price'; it is better to debit the cash price and treat the interest separately, because the interest is a financing cost, not part of the asset.
A company buys a van for ₦900,000 on instalment: ₦300,000 now, and ₦300,000 at the end of each of the next two years, plus interest of ₦30,000 a year paid with each instalment.

Purchase: Dr Van 900,000; Cr Creditor 900,000. Payment now: Dr Creditor 300,000; Cr Bank 300,000. End of year 1: Dr Creditor 300,000, Dr Interest expense 30,000; Cr Bank 330,000. End of year 2: the same.

p: A buyer with a low income and little trust from sellers may find hire purchase easier. A buyer who wants ownership at once (for example to modify or sell the item) and has good credit may prefer an instalment sale. A seller who fears default prefers hire purchase because the goods can be taken back.

Gross profit = net sales – cost of goods sold. COGS = opening stock + purchases + carriage inwards – closing stock. Net profit = gross profit + other income – expenses. Closing capital = opening capital + net profit – drawings. Assets = liabilities + capital. Hire purchase price = deposit + instalments. Interest = hire purchase price – cash price.
